From Grebe

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch the squares and the long lines follow them.
How to play: Drag a corner with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys. Tick “Show names” to see what each point is called.
Look for the math

Put a square on each side of a triangle. The far sides of those squares meet in a second triangle, and lines joining matching corners all pass through one point. From that point the original triangle can be found again. Drag a corner and see whether any of this breaks.

Squares on all three sides

Start with the triangle the page calls A'B'C' (the dots you can drag). On each side the applet builds a square by turning the side a quarter turn. The side of each square furthest from the triangle is drawn as a long dashed line. Those three lines meet at A0, B0 and C0. The turn is always the same way round, so if you drag a corner across a side and the triangle winds the other way, the squares lie inside it instead of outside. That is a quirk of the old applet, kept here on purpose.

Three lines, one point

Grebe noticed in 1847 that A'A0, B'B0 and C'C0 all pass through the same point K. For a triangle with sides a, b, c, that point has barycentric coordinates a² : b² : c². It is the symmedian point, also called the Lemoine point. Tick “Show names” to see K's fellow points; the three joining lines are drawn dashed through it.

A copy at a fixed scale

Now draw the lines from K to the two far corners of each square. Where they cut the side of A'B'C', turn that short segment a quarter turn: the new point is a corner of square ABC, shown in green. Everything here is a homothety centred at K. If D is twice the signed area of A'B'C' and S = a²+b²+c², then ABC = K + r(A' − K) with r = D / (D − S), while A0B0C0 uses 1/r. For the winding that puts the squares outside, r = 2·area / (S + 2·area). Since r is fixed by the shape, the answer is determined uniquely. When the winding flips, r becomes negative: the green triangle turns up on the other side of K.

What was checked

The logic test runs 33 checks: the opening triangle, eight hand-picked shapes and 600 random ones. In every case the three joining lines really meet, the meeting point has coordinates a²:b²:c², and both outer and inner triangles sit on the same rays from K with the stated scale. Every constructed point is also compared with a second transcription of the applet's own Compute(), GetSquare(), Rotate() and Intersect() bytecode. The live cut-the-knot page still embeds this Java applet, and its notation is followed here: the draggable triangle is A'B'C', the reconstructed one is ABC. The page's story about Dodgson's Pillow Problems and the Ladies' Diary is history, not an extra rule.

Drag C across the line A'B'. Watch K and the green triangle jump to the other side while the three lines still meet exactly there.
